title: A second is defined using 9,192,631,770 cycles
body: The international second is defined by setting the frequency of a particular transition in a caesium-133 atom to exactly 9,192,631,770 cycles per second. Atomic clocks tune a signal to match that transition.
takeaway: A unit of time can be reproduced with the same kind of atom in laboratories far apart.
source: US National Institute of Standards and Technology, Meet the Constants
visual: a caesium atomic clock with a softly lit vacuum chamber

title: The metre is defined by how far light travels
body: Since 1983 the metre has been tied to light's speed in a vacuum, set exactly at 299,792,458 metres per second. A metre is the distance light travels in one of that many equal slices of a second.
takeaway: Any laboratory that can reproduce the second can, in principle, realise the same unit of length.
source: US National Institute of Standards and Technology, Defining the International System of Units
visual: a narrow beam crossing a dark optical bench between two mirrors

title: A volcanic eruption can send a raft of rock across the sea
body: In 1979 a pumice raft was the first sign of an eruption near Metis Shoal in Tonga. Pumice contains many gas pockets, so pieces of the rock can float and gather in a broad layer on the ocean.
takeaway: Floating fragments can reveal an underwater eruption before its source is visible.
source: US Geological Survey, Volcano Watch: Metis Shoal, Tonga
visual: a field of light pumice fragments drifting together on dark ocean water
